newsitem.title: UK: Sterling solid against mark but dependent on dlr.
newsitem.headline: Sterling solid against mark but dependent on dlr.

text.p: Sterling made modest gains against the mark in Europe, spurred on by a firmer dollar/mark and concerns about the strength of the new single European currency after Sunday's first-round French election, analysts said.

The French franc has eased on worries France's Socialist-led coalition of parties, which outpolled the centre-right ruling coalition in Sunday's vote, may win the election outright and its demands for a softer EMU could upset the whole project.
"I think at the moment sterling is benefiting from some uncertainty over the French election," said Lee Ferridge, currency strategist at Commerzbank.
In early European trade, sterling/mark was at 2.7732/37 up from 2.7716/21 at the previous close.
Analysts did not think any flow of funds from France and the generally weaker tone in the mark would be sustained. Sterling's rally could be short lived as a result, they said.
"I don't think it is going to last that long," Ferridge said of the rally, which followed a two-day tumble late last week.
"If the French franc and the lira and the others come under real pressure, then you would expect the mark to strengthen across the board," he added.
A premium had been built into sterling from being outside the EMU process, analysts said, and any hint that it would not go ahead could damage sterling while the mark strengthened.
A strong dollar also helped drag sterling higher against the mark in morning trade.
"Sterling/mark has done well because the dollar's done well," one trader said. "That's the general foible of the market at the moment. Sterling/mark has been pulled up by the dollar."
But the dollar's strength hit cable early on before a slight lapse in the U.S. unit's strength allowed sterling to inch higher and reach 1.6353, down from 1.6398 at the previous close.
Overnight, traders had looked to reported comments from new U.K. trade chief Margaret Beckett that there was a possibilty Britain would rejoin the European exchange rate mechanism.

Sterling came under some selling pressure against the yen in the far east but here traders and analysts said the market had largely ignored the reported comments, which the UK Treasury denied Beckett had said.
"The market seems to have disgarded that and moved back up again on the back of other currencies," said Dharshini David, U.K. economist at HSBC markets.
